usage: Korean summer's sticky heat that clings to your skin; the go-to July–August complaint
polite present; say it when you step outside and the air feels like a wet towel
modifier -ㄴ attaches to the stem before a noun; describes the kind of day
-아/어서 reason form; natural lead-in to '에어컨 켰어요 (I turned on the AC)'
examples: 오늘 좀 후텁지근하네요.
It's a bit muggy today.
the bare minimum small-talk line; -네요 reacts to what you feel right now
장마철이라 그런지 방 안이 너무 후텁지근해요.
Maybe because it's monsoon season, the room is so muggy.
장마철 (rainy season) is the prime context; -(이)라 그런지 = 'maybe because'
밖에 나가자마자 후텁지근해서 바로 다시 들어왔어.
The second I stepped outside it was so muggy I came right back in.
casual 반말; -자마자 = 'the moment that', capturing the wall-of-humidity feeling
nuance: 후텁지근하다 names heat AND humidity together — the heavy, steamy, clothes-sticking-to-skin air of a Korean summer night, not just a high number on the thermometer. The sharp contrast is with plain 덥다 (simply 'hot', could be dry desert heat) and with 무덥다 (also oppressive but a touch more formal/written); 후텁지근하다 is the spoken, sensory, slightly whiny word you use when the muggy air actually bothers you. It collocates with 날씨, 방 안, 공기, and especially 장마철. The English-speaker trap is reaching for it whenever it's 'hot' — if there's no stickiness, it must be 덥다, because the whole point of this word is the wet, suffocating quality. Also watch the spelling: standard is 후텁지근하다 (not 후덥지근하다), even though it relates to 덥다.

mistakes: Using it for dry heat: a sunny but dry 28°C day is 덥다, not 후텁지근하다 — this word requires humidity, so reserve it for sticky, sweaty air.
Spelling it 후덥지근하다 by analogy with 덥다; the dictionary-standard form is 후텁지근하다 with ㅌ.
Saying '나는 후텁지근해요' to mean 'I feel hot/sweaty' — the subject is the air or the weather, not a person; for yourself say 덥다 or 땀나다.

usage: the brisk cool of early morning or late autumn; not freezing, just jacket-weather
polite present; the default spring/fall weather small talk
modifier -ㄴ before a noun; also 쌀쌀한 바람 (a chilly wind)
set phrase for the daily temperature swing (일교차)
examples: 오늘 좀 쌀쌀해요.
It's a bit chilly today.
the simplest version; 좀 softens it to 'a little'
요즘 아침저녁으로 쌀쌀하니까 겉옷 챙기세요.
These days it's chilly morning and evening, so take a jacket.
-(으)니까 gives the reason for advice; classic seasonal line you'll hear constantly
바람까지 부니까 생각보다 훨씬 쌀쌀하네요.
With the wind blowing too, it's way chillier than I expected.
-까지 ('even/on top of that') stacks the wind onto the cold; -네요 for in-the-moment reaction
nuance: 쌀쌀하다 is a mild, brisk chill — the kind that makes you reach for a light jacket or cardigan, the signature feeling of spring mornings and autumn evenings. The dividing line you must learn: 쌀쌀하다 (cool, jacket weather) < 싸늘하다 (genuinely cold, often eerie) < 춥다 (cold, the all-purpose word) < 매섭다 (painfully biting winter cold). So if your teeth chatter, it's already past 쌀쌀하다. A second, equally common use is about people: 쌀쌀하다 / 쌀쌀맞다 / 쌀쌀하게 대하다 describe a cold, aloof, standoffish attitude — context (weather vs. a person) tells you which. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as 'cold'; it is deliberately understated, closer to 'a bit nippy', and overusing it for real cold sounds off.

Treating it as a synonym of 싸늘하다; 싸늘하다 is colder and can feel eerie/tense, whereas 쌀쌀하다 is just pleasantly brisk.
Forgetting the personality meaning: '그 사람 좀 쌀쌀해' means 'that person is a bit cold/distant', not that they feel cool to the touch.

usage: gently warm — a winter day milder than usual, or a soft, snug feeling
polite present; said with relief when winter cold eases
modifier -ㄴ before a noun; also 포근한 이불 (a cozy blanket)
날(이) + adjective is a very natural weather frame
examples: 오늘은 좀 포근하네요.
It's a bit mild today.
the basic line; perfect when a cold spell suddenly softens
한겨울인데도 날이 포근해서 산책 나왔어요.
Even though it's midwinter, the day's so mild I came out for a walk.
-(으)ㄴ데도 = 'even though'; the textbook context of a surprisingly warm winter day
이불이 포근해서 도저히 못 일어나겠어.
The blanket's so cozy I just can't get up.
반말; shows the 'soft & snug' object sense — 도저히 + 못 = 'no way can I'
nuance: 포근하다 carries warmth wrapped in comfort — most often a winter day that turns out gentler than expected, or soft, snuggly things like 이불 (blankets), 옷, and a mother's hug. The key contrast is with 따뜻하다, which is the neutral, all-temperature 'warm'; 포근하다 adds emotion — you say it with relief, contentment, or affection, never about plain heat. It pairs with 날씨, 날, 이불, 분위기, 품 (embrace). Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, do not use it for summer warmth or any strong heat — it is reserved for gentle, mild warmth, so a hot day is 덥다, never 포근하다. Second, do not limit it to weather: '이불이 포근하다' (the blanket is cozy) is just as natural and very common.

Assuming it equals 따뜻하다: 따뜻하다 is the neutral 'warm', while 포근하다 always adds a cozy, emotionally positive feeling.
Limiting it to weather and missing the object use; '포근한 스웨터/이불' (a cozy sweater/blanket) is an everyday, natural collocation.

usage: intense, oppressive, usually humid summer heat; ㅂ-irregular stem
the forecast staple: 무더위가 계속되다 (the heat wave continues)
examples: 오늘 진짜 무덥네요.
It's really sweltering today.
the simple reaction line; 진짜 adds 'really'
무더운 날에는 수분 섭취가 정말 중요해요.
On sweltering days, staying hydrated is really important.
newscast-style advice; 무더운 날 = a sweltering day
밤에도 안 식어서 무더운 열대야가 계속되고 있어요.
It doesn't even cool down at night, so the sweltering tropical nights keep going.
열대야 ('tropical night') pairs naturally with 무덥다; -고 있다 for an ongoing stretch
nuance: 무덥다 is heat with weight — heavy, stifling, energy-draining, almost always with humidity behind it, a clear step above plain 덥다. The 무- here is the intensifying/heavy 'mu-', so think 'heavily hot'. Contrast: 덥다 = neutral 'hot' (any hot), 무덥다 = oppressively, stiflingly hot, and the spoken/sensory cousin 후텁지근하다 leans on the sticky muggy feel while 무덥다 sounds a notch more standard and is the form used in forecasts and writing. Its noun 무더위 appears all over summer weather reports (무더위 특보, 무더위가 기승을 부리다). The two pitfalls: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — it is 무더워요/무더운/무더위, never 무덥어요/무덥은; (2) don't downgrade it to mild warmth — 무덥다 is reserved for genuinely draining heat, so a pleasantly warm day is 따뜻하다, not 무덥다.

mistakes: Conjugating it regularly as 무덥어요/무덥은; it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct forms are 무더워요 and 무더운.
Using it for mild or pleasant warmth: 무덥다 is intense, stifling heat — a nice warm day is 따뜻하다, and a merely hot day is 덥다.
Forgetting the high-frequency noun 무더위; in forecasts you'll hear 무더위가 계속되다/기승을 부리다 far more than the adjective.

usage: comfortable coolness, especially early autumn after the summer heat breaks
polite present; said with relief as the weather turns nice
선선한 most often pairs with 바람 (breeze) or 날씨/공기
examples: 이제 좀 선선해요.
It's pleasantly cool now.
the basic line; 이제 ('now') signals the season has turned
아침 공기가 선선해서 산책하기 딱 좋아요.
The morning air is so cool that it's just right for a walk.
딱 좋다 = 'just right'; -기 좋다 = 'good for ~ing'
더위가 한풀 꺾이고 드디어 선선해졌네요.
The heat has eased off and it's finally turned cool.
한풀 꺾이다 = '(heat) to die down', a very Korean expression; 드디어 = 'finally'
nuance: 선선하다 is pleasant, refreshing coolness — the welcome relief when summer finally lets go and early autumn arrives, the temperature where you feel comfortable without a jacket. It is always positive, which is exactly the dividing line from its neighbors: 선선하다 (nice, comfortable cool) → 쌀쌀하다 (chilly enough to want a jacket) → 싸늘하다 (uncomfortably, sharply cold). So once you actually feel cold, you have left 선선하다 behind. It collocates with 바람, 날씨, 공기, 가을 and very often appears as 선선해지다 to mark the change of season, or with 한풀 꺾이다 (the heat dying down). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'cool' too literally and applying it to genuinely cold weather, or pairing it with ongoing summer heat — 선선하다 inherently implies the heat has already passed and what's left feels good.

mistakes: Using it when it's actually cold: 선선하다 means comfortable, refreshing cool — if you need a jacket, that's 쌀쌀하다, not 선선하다.
Pairing it with peak summer: saying '여름이 선선해요' clashes, because 선선하다 implies the heat has already eased; use it for early autumn or cool evenings.
Confusing it with 시원하다: 시원하다 is the broad 'refreshing/cool' (drinks, AC, relief), while 선선하다 is specifically the pleasant coolness of the air/weather.

usage: bright, beautiful blue-sky weather; the ideal day to go out
polite present; a cheerful weather report
화창한 + 날씨/봄날 are the typical pairings
examples: 오늘 날씨 화창하네요.
The weather's lovely and sunny today.
the simple delighted reaction; note 날씨(가) often drops 가 in speech
날씨가 화창해서 한강 가기 딱 좋아요.
The weather's so nice and sunny it's perfect for going to the Han River.
-아서 reason + -기 좋다; 화창한 날 is when everyone heads to 한강
내일은 미세먼지도 없고 하늘이 화창할 거래요.
They say tomorrow there'll be no fine dust and the sky will be clear and sunny.
-(이)래요 reports a forecast; 미세먼지 (fine dust) is a real daily concern in Korea
nuance: 화창하다 describes bright, clear, beautiful weather — sunny skies, fresh air, the kind of day that lifts your mood, classically a spring or autumn 'perfect day'. It is Sino-Korean: 和 (hwa, 'harmonious/gentle') + 暢 (chang, 'flowing freely/unobstructed'), so the image is of mild, freely bright, unblocked weather. The contrast to learn: 맑다 just means 'clear' (sky, water, even sound) and is purely about clarity, while 화창하다 adds warmth, brightness and a pleasant mood — a clear but bitterly cold winter sky is 맑다, not 화창하다. It pairs with 날씨, 봄날, 하늘, 가을. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use it merely for 'not raining' — cloudy-but-dry is not 화창하다; and it describes daytime brightness, so it doesn't fit a clear night sky (for that, 맑다).

Treating it as identical to 맑다: 맑다 is plain clarity (it can be clear but freezing), whereas 화창하다 adds warm, cheerful brightness, so a cold clear day is 맑다.
Applying it to night: 화창하다 is about daytime brightness; a clear night sky is 하늘이 맑다, not 화창하다.

usage: high moisture in the air; the defining feature of Korean summer and the rainy season
polite present; also said of a damp room or basement
습한 before a noun; also 습한 공기 (damp air)
습하다 + 덥다 is the classic Korean-summer combo
examples: 오늘 좀 습하네요.
It's a bit humid today.
the bare small-talk line; you'll feel it before you see it
장마철엔 너무 습해서 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
During the rainy season it's so humid the laundry won't dry well.
a very real apartment-life problem; -아서 links cause to result
방이 습한 것 같아서 제습기를 틀었어.
The room felt damp so I turned on the dehumidifier.
반말; 제습기 (dehumidifier) is a summer essential — -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 = 'seems'
nuance: 습하다 is about moisture in the air, deliberately separate from temperature — you can have a 습한 but cool, clammy day (a damp basement, a rainy spring). It is Sino-Korean from 濕 ('wet/damp'), and its exact opposite is 건조하다 (dry, from 乾燥). In Korea it is the word behind summer misery: 빨래가 안 마르다 (laundry won't dry), 곰팡이 (mold), and the constant hum of the 제습기 (dehumidifier). The crucial English-speaker pitfall is collapsing it into 'hot': 습하다 means humid, not hot — they merely co-occur in summer, so a cool damp day is still 습하다, and a dry hot desert day is 덥다 but absolutely not 습하다. Keep the pair straight: 습하다 (humid) ↔ 건조하다 (dry), and pair 습하다 with 덥다 only when both are true.

Using it for dry conditions: the opposite of 습하다 is 건조하다, so a dry winter day is 건조하다, never 습하다.
Forgetting the indoor/room use: '방/지하실이 습하다' (the room/basement is damp) is just as common as talking about the weather.

usage: low humidity in the air; the hallmark of Korean winter and spring
polite present; also used for dry skin (피부가 건조해요)
건조한 before a noun; also 건조한 공기/피부
a real fire-risk warning issued in dry seasons (건조주의보가 내려지다)
examples: 요즘 너무 건조해요.
It's so dry these days.
the simple seasonal complaint, peak winter
날씨가 건조해서 입술이 자꾸 트네요.
The weather's so dry my lips keep chapping.
트다 = (skin/lips) to chap; -아서 cause, -네요 reaction
피부가 건조할 땐 자기 전에 로션을 꼭 발라요.
When my skin is dry, I always put on lotion before bed.
shows the skin use; -(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when', 꼭 = 'without fail'
nuance: 건조하다 is the dryness of low-humidity air — the exact opposite of 습하다 — typical of Korean winter and the spring fire-warning season, when 가습기 (humidifiers) come out and 건조주의보 (dry-weather advisories) get issued. It is Sino-Korean: 乾 (geon, 'dry/heaven') + 燥 (jo, 'parched'), literally 'dried and parched'. Its range is wide: equally natural for skin (피부가 건조하다, 입술이 트다) and even for a person's manner or a piece of writing — 건조한 말투/문체 means a dry, flat, emotionless tone. The two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) don't mix it up with 습하다 — they are antonyms, 건조하다 = dry, 습하다 = humid; (2) don't box it into weather only, since 'my skin is dry' (피부가 건조해요) is one of its most everyday uses, and the metaphorical 'dry/dull' sense is common too.

usage: piercing winter cold or a sharp, cutting wind; ㅂ-irregular stem
매서운 + 바람/추위 are the standard pairings
examples: 오늘 바람 진짜 매섭네요.
The wind is really biting today.
the simple reaction; 진짜 adds force, -네요 reacts on the spot
추위가 매서우니까 패딩 단단히 입고 나가세요.
The cold is biting, so bundle up well in your padded coat before you go.
-(으)니까 reason for advice; 패딩 (padded coat) is the Korean winter uniform
한파에 칼바람까지 매섭게 불어서 귀가 다 얼었어.
On top of the cold wave, a knife-sharp wind blew bitterly and my ears froze solid.
반말; 칼바람 (knife wind) + 매섭다 is very natural, -까지 stacks the wind on the cold wave
nuance: 매섭다 describes a fierce, piercing, almost painful quality — most often a biting winter wind or a sharp cold that hurts exposed skin, the harshest end of the cold scale (쌀쌀하다 → 싸늘하다 → 춥다 → 매섭다). Its core sense isn't temperature but 'cutting/severe', which is why it transfers to people: 매서운 눈빛 (a piercing, fierce stare), 매섭게 몰아붙이다 (to scold/press sharply). It collocates with 바람, 추위, 한파, 칼바람, 눈빛. Two things trip English speakers up: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — it is 매서워요/매서운/매섭게, never 매섭어요/매섭은; (2) don't use it for ordinary cold — 매섭다 is reserved for harsh, biting, painful cold or wind, so a merely cold day is 춥다 and a mildly chilly one is 쌀쌀하다, with 매섭다 saved for when the wind actually stings.

usage: the soft, comforting warmth of sunshine; ㅂ-irregular stem
the natural subject is sunlight, not air temperature
examples: 햇살이 참 따사로워요.
The sunshine is so warm and gentle.
the simple admiring line; 참 = 'truly', a soft intensifier
봄 햇살이 따사로워서 벤치에 한참 앉아 있었어요.
The spring sunshine was so gentle and warm that I sat on the bench for a long while.
-아서 cause; 한참 = 'for a good while', the cozy basking feeling
겨울인데도 창으로 따사로운 볕이 들어와서 마음까지 포근해졌어.
Even in winter, gentle sun came through the window and even my heart felt cozy.
반말; 볕이 들다 = 'sun shines in', -까지 extends the warmth to the heart
nuance: 따사롭다 is the softer, more poetic cousin of 따뜻하다, used almost exclusively for sunlight (햇살, 햇볕, 볕) and, by extension, warm-hearted feelings (따사로운 미소, 따사로운 정). Where 따뜻하다 is the everyday, all-purpose 'warm' (warm water, a warm room, a warm person), 따사롭다 specifically evokes a gentle, soothing, slightly literary warmth and a peaceful mood — which is why you meet it in captions, lyrics, essays, and heartfelt speech far more than in plain weather chat. It collocates above all with 햇살/햇볕/볕, and with 미소, 정, 손길. Two pitfalls: (1) the ㅂ-irregular — 따사로워요/따사로운, never 따사롭어요/따사롭은; (2) don't use it for general air temperature or to describe how warm a room or drink is — for that you want 따뜻하다, because 따사롭다 is tied to the gentle warmth of sunshine.

usage: a sharper, colder chill than 쌀쌀하다; air that's gone genuinely cold
polite present; said when the temperature has clearly dropped
싸늘한 + 공기/날씨; also 싸늘한 분위기 (a tense, frosty mood)
-아/어지다; weather or a mood suddenly going cold
examples: 밤엔 좀 싸늘해요.
It's a bit cold at night.
the simple line; the chill that comes after dark
해가 지니까 공기가 갑자기 싸늘해졌어요.
Once the sun set, the air suddenly turned cold.
-(으)니까 cause-then-effect; -아지다 marks the change to cold
내 농담 한마디에 분위기가 싸늘해졌어.
One joke from me and the mood turned ice-cold.
반말; the very common figurative use — a frozen, awkward atmosphere after a flat joke
nuance: 싸늘하다 is colder and sharper than 쌀쌀하다, frequently with an unsettling or tense edge — think air that has gone abruptly cold after sunset, or the chill of a too-quiet room. Placed on the cold scale it sits 쌀쌀하다 (mild, jacket weather) < 싸늘하다 (genuinely cold, often eerie) < 춥다/매섭다. But its most useful everyday life is figurative: 분위기가 싸늘하다 / 싸늘해지다 describes a room going awkwardly silent, frosty, or hostile — the classic case being right after someone tells a joke that bombs (썰렁하다 is the lighter 'lame/cringe' version; 싸늘하다 is the heavier 'frozen, hostile' one). It pairs with 공기, 날씨, 새벽, 시선, 반응, 분위기. The pitfalls: don't equate it with 쌀쌀하다 (싸늘하다 is colder and tenser), and don't miss the atmosphere meaning, which natives use constantly.

mistakes: Treating it as identical to 쌀쌀하다: 싸늘하다 is noticeably colder and often carries an eerie or tense feeling, while 쌀쌀하다 is just mildly brisk.

usage: vivid idiom: heat so heavy the air feels steamed; standard spacing is 푹푹 찌다
pairs with 더위 (heat) for peak-summer days
examples: 밖에 완전 푹푹 쪄요.
It's totally boiling outside.
the everyday exaggeration; 완전 ('totally') is casual intensifier slang
에어컨 없이는 푹푹 찌는 여름을 도저히 못 버텨요.
Without AC, there's no way I can survive the sweltering summer.
버티다 = to endure; 찌는 modifies 여름, 도저히 + 못 = 'simply can't'
삼복더위라 그런지 아침부터 푹푹 찌네.
Maybe because it's the dog days of summer, it's been sweltering since morning.
반말; 삼복더위 = the hottest stretch (복날), -아서 그런지 = 'maybe because'
nuance: 푹푹 찌다 literally means '(the heat) steams you' — 찌다 is the verb 'to steam', and the mimetic 푹푹 paints heat pressing down in thick waves, so the whole phrase is an idiomatic, highly colloquial way to say it's brutally, oppressively hot. It outranks even 무덥다 in vividness and feeling, and unlike the other items here it is a verb phrase, not a single adjective, so it conjugates on 찌다 (쪄요, 찌는, 쪘어요). You'll hear it everywhere in a Korean heat wave, paired with 더위, 날씨, 여름. Two real pitfalls: (1) 찌다 is a homophone minefield — the same 찌다 means 'to gain weight' (살이 찌다) and 'to steam food' (만두를 찌다), so only the weather context (날씨/더위/밖) tells you it's 'sweltering'; (2) spacing — the standard written form keeps a space, 푹푹 찌다, not 푹푹찌다.
